description: The chase. The mouse comes out on his errand and the cat gets up and goes after him — genuinely: the cat's destination is the mouse's LIVE position, re-read four times a second (Josh's call, 2026-09-06). What is shared is the decision — that a hunt happens, at this second, for this long; the path each viewer sees is their own, exactly as a local trigger's response is. The mouse track leads by two seconds so there is prey on the floor before the cat is asked to hunt: npc/cat/hunt REFUSES when the floor is empty, and that refusal is logged rather than played as a cat stalking nothing. ★ THE RATE IS AUTHORED AGAINST A DWELL, NOT AGAINST A DAY (Josh, 2026-09-07: watched for minutes, saw the mouse cycle twice and the cat never leave the bed). It first shipped at a 1500 s mean gap, and because this event is exclusive on BOTH channels — and the schema DROPS a blocked event rather than queueing it — the mouse channel being busy 22% of the time (mouse_errand, 46 s on a 210 s gap) plus mouse_belt_run's 6.5% turned that into an effective 36 MINUTES between chases. The row's headline beat was invisible to any realistic viewer. 480/260 lands it at roughly one chase every 11 minutes after collisions, so a 30-minute dwell contains two or three. Re-check this arithmetic whenever mouse_errand's gap or duration moves — the collision rate is what binds here, not the authored gap. ★ AND THE ESCAPE IS NOT SCRIPTED HERE. An earlier cut carried a npc/mouse/flee track at +34 s as well as the proximity reflex, which is TWO MECHANISMS FOR ONE BEAT: a fixed timestamp cannot know whether the cat ever got close, so the mouse bolted on schedule whether or not anything was chasing him — and it fired after a pounce had already resolved the chase, yanking him into the wall for no visible reason. mouse_bolt (local, on proximity) owns the escape; this event only sets the hunt up and calls it off.
